Guide

Why we won't say "therapeutic grade"

Last updated 26 October 2026

It appears on bottles everywhere and it means nothing. No body awards it, no standard defines it, and no test can confirm it. Here is what to look for instead.

Walk down any aisle selling essential oils and you will see the same phrase on half the bottles: therapeutic grade. Sometimes certified therapeutic grade. Occasionally, with real confidence, clinical grade.

None of it means anything. There is no body that awards the designation, no standard that defines it, and no laboratory test that can confirm a bottle qualifies. A company can print it on a label because it decided to.

Why the phrase exists

It exists because buyers reasonably want a quality signal, and the industry has no consumer-facing one to give. Food has FSSAI. Organic produce has certifying bodies. Essential oils sit in a regulatory gap — they are not food, not cosmetics in most uses, and not medicines. So the gap got filled with marketing.

That is not to say every brand using the phrase is cutting their oils. Most are not. But the phrase itself tells you nothing about whether they are, which makes it useless for the one job you want it to do.

What is actually worth looking at

Four things on a label tell you more than any grading claim.

  • The botanical name. "Lavender" covers at least three different plants at three different prices. Lavandula angustifolia is the one most people mean. If a bottle will not tell you the species, ask why.
  • The country of origin. Not because one country is better, but because a supplier who knows where an oil came from is a supplier with a real chain behind them.
  • The extraction method. Steam distilled, cold pressed, CO2 extracted or solvent extracted are genuinely different products with different characteristics and prices.
  • The part of the plant. Cinnamon bark and cinnamon leaf are not the same oil and are not equally safe. Clove bud, leaf and stem differ in both quality and harshness.

A bottle that gives you all four is telling you something checkable. A bottle that gives you a grading phrase instead is telling you something that cannot be checked at all.

The price question

Price is an imperfect signal but not a useless one. Rose, sandalwood, melissa and Roman chamomile are expensive because of yield — the volume of plant material needed per bottle is enormous, and no amount of efficient production changes that.

So when every oil on a shelf costs roughly the same, something is wrong. Either the cheap ones are overpriced, or the expensive ones are not what they say. A range with a genuine spread from a few hundred rupees to several thousand is a range that is probably being honest about what is in each bottle.

What we say instead

Our oils are pure and undiluted, with no synthetic fragrance or fillers. We ask our suppliers for the documentation that accompanies each batch, and we will share it if you ask.

What we will not do is dress that up into something grander. We are a young business with a deliberately small range, and we would rather tell you precisely what we know than invent a certification to stand behind. If you want to know exactly what we hold on a particular oil, ask us and we will tell you straight.
